title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
setting: Boston in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, in the 1640s, reached through a Salem custom house of the 1840s
lengthNote: Twenty-four chapters, preceded by an introductory sketch nearly a sixth of the book's length
openingLine: A throng of bearded men, in sad-colored garments, and gray, steeple-crowned hats, intermixed with women, some wearing hoods and others bareheaded, was assembled in front of a wooden edifice, the door of which was heavily timbered with oak, and studded with iron spikes.
summary: A woman is sentenced to wear an embroidered letter for the rest of her life, refuses to name the father of her child, and outlives the sentence without ever being released from it. Hawthorne is less interested in the adultery, which has already happened when the book opens, than in what seven years of public meaning does to four people: the woman who is marked, the minister who is not, the husband who uses diagnosis as revenge, and the child who is made to stand for all of it.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Scarlet Letter
sourceText.note: References give the chapter, or the introductory sketch, which this text titles 'The Customhouse'.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Ticknor, Reed and Fields, Boston. A second edition followed within weeks.

atAGlance.label: Called
atAGlance.note: Hawthorne's own subtitle, and a claim about the kind of truth the book is offering.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Daylight, midnight, daylight — the book's structure is a stage used three times.

atAGlance.label: Span
atAGlance.note: From Pearl at three months old to the Election Day sermon.

atAGlance.label: Frame
atAGlance.note: A sketch of Hawthorne's own surveyorship, which invents an archival source for everything that follows.

structure.label: The Customhouse
structure.title: Hawthorne at the Salem Custom House
structure.summary: A surveyor of customs at Salem describes the dozing office he worked in and the parcel he claims to have turned up in the upper storey: a worn scrap of embroidered cloth and some papers about the woman who wore it. He puts the letter on his own breast and feels it burn. Every document in this sketch is invented, and in the sketch Hawthorne is honest about invention.

scenes.title: The upper storey
scenes.summary: The narrator finds the rag of scarlet cloth and Surveyor Pue's papers, and takes the burn on his chest as a commission.

structure.label: Chapters 1–8
structure.title: The prison door and the first scaffold
structure.summary: Hester Prynne comes out of the jail with a three-month-old child and a letter she has embroidered far beyond the sentence. She refuses to name the father while he stands above her on the balcony and asks her to. In the crowd is the husband nobody has seen for two years, who makes her swear to keep his identity secret and settles into Boston as a physician.

scenes.title: The Marketplace
scenes.summary: Hester emerges with Pearl and the letter, and the women of the town discuss what a proper punishment would have been.

scenes.title: The Recognition
scenes.summary: Dimmesdale is ordered to exhort her to name her partner; she refuses him to his face.

scenes.title: The Interview
scenes.summary: In the prison Chillingworth binds her to silence about his name and swears to find the man.

scenes.title: The Elf-Child and the Minister
scenes.summary: The magistrates consider removing Pearl; Hester appeals to Dimmesdale, who argues successfully for her.

structure.label: Chapters 9–12
structure.title: The physician moves in
structure.summary: Chillingworth attaches himself to the failing minister as doctor and lodger, and begins an investigation conducted entirely through sympathy. Dimmesdale's sermons grow more powerful as his health collapses; he scourges himself in a locked closet and cannot say the one sentence that would end it. At last he climbs the scaffold at midnight, where nobody can see him confess.

scenes.title: The Leech and His Patient
scenes.summary: Chillingworth opens the sleeping minister's vestment and sees something on his chest; the narrator does not say what.

scenes.title: The Interior of a Heart
scenes.summary: The more Dimmesdale accuses himself in the pulpit in general terms, the holier his congregation thinks him.

scenes.title: The Minister's Vigil
scenes.summary: A midnight confession with an audience of three, a meteor in the shape of a letter, and a glove left on the scaffold.

structure.label: Chapters 13–15
structure.title: Hester seven years on
structure.summary: Hester has become the town's unpaid nurse, and the townspeople have begun to read her letter as 'Able'. Hawthorne notes what that respectability has cost: passion turned into thought, a woman who now speculates freely because she has nothing left to lose socially. She confronts Chillingworth, tells him she means to break her promise, and looks at what he has become.

scenes.title: Another View of Hester
scenes.summary: The letter’s meaning has drifted, and the narrator sets out what the change has cost Hester.

scenes.title: Hester and the Physician
scenes.summary: She releases herself from her oath; he declines to forgive and calls it fate.

scenes.title: Hester and Pearl
scenes.summary: Hester admits to herself that she hates her husband, and Pearl asks what the letter means.

structure.label: Chapters 16–19
structure.title: The meeting in the forest
structure.summary: Hester intercepts Dimmesdale on a forest path, tells him who the physician is, and is forgiven. They plan a ship to Europe. She throws the letter into the leaves, lets down her hair, and the sunshine arrives on cue — until Pearl, on the far bank of a brook, refuses to cross until her mother puts the letter back on.

scenes.title: The Pastor and His Parishioner
scenes.summary: Two people who have not spoken in seven years argue about what their sin actually was.

scenes.title: A Flood of Sunshine
scenes.summary: The letter comes off and the forest changes lighting.

scenes.title: The Child at the Brook-Side
scenes.summary: Pearl will not recognise a mother without the letter, and screams until it is fastened on again.

structure.label: Chapters 20–24
structure.title: Election Day
structure.summary: Dimmesdale walks back through the town nearly deranged with the effort of pretending, writes the sermon of his life in one night, and preaches it. Then he asks Hester and Pearl to help him onto the scaffold in daylight, tells the colony what he is, tears open his shirt and dies. The witnesses immediately begin to disagree about what they saw.

scenes.title: The New England Holiday
scenes.summary: The whole colony gathers; Hester learns that Chillingworth has taken passage on the same ship.

scenes.title: The Revelation of the Scarlet Letter
scenes.summary: The confession, the chest, and Chillingworth's collapse.

scenes.title: Conclusion
scenes.summary: Several accounts of what was on the minister's breast, Pearl's inheritance and marriage abroad, and Hester's return to resume the letter voluntarily.

characters.name: Hester Prynne
characters.role: A needleworker sentenced to wear the letter A
characters.summary: She is the only person in the book who never lies, and the only one who is punished. Left to support a child on embroidery, she gradually makes herself indispensable to the town that sentenced her, and the change in her — from passion to speculation, from beauty to a kind of marble calm — is described by the narrator as a loss, not a triumph.
characters.clue: She embroiders her own sentence in gold thread, refuses for seven years to name the man, and comes back at the end to put the badge on again when nobody is making her.

characters.name: Arthur Dimmesdale
characters.summary: A young clergyman of great ability whose sermons improve in exact proportion as his health fails, because the congregation hears the suffering and mistakes it for holiness. He confesses constantly in terms so general that every confession makes him more revered, and the novel is merciless about how comfortable that arrangement is.
characters.clue: He keeps his hand over his heart, preaches better the worse he gets, and confesses at midnight where nobody can hear.

characters.name: Roger Chillingworth
characters.role: Physician, and Hester's husband under another name
characters.summary: A scholar who sent a much younger wife ahead to a colony and arrived two years late to find her on a scaffold. He is right about everything — he identifies the man, he reads the symptoms, he proves his case — and the book treats the accuracy as the crime, because he uses a doctor's access to get inside a heart and stay there.
characters.clue: He arrives from the forest with one shoulder higher than the other, takes a new name at the prison door, and spends seven years being right.

characters.name: Pearl
characters.summary: Adults keep calling her a symbol — the scarlet letter given life, a demon child, evidence of sin — and she keeps behaving like a bright, neglected, furiously observant little girl. Her questions are the most exact in the book precisely because nobody has taught her what may not be asked.
characters.clue: Dressed in scarlet and gold to match her mother's badge, she throws flowers at it, and will not cross a brook until it is put back on.

characters.name: The Surveyor of Customs
characters.summary: A version of Hawthorne who spent three years counting cargo, lost the job to a change of administration, and claims to have found the story in an attic. He is the reason the book is called a romance, not a history: he hands the reader a forged provenance and says so in the same breath.
characters.clue: He is dismissed from a government post, blames the guillotine of politics, and produces a manuscript nobody else has ever seen.

relationships.label: claims to have found the papers about

characters.name: Governor Bellingham
characters.summary: He owns the grandest house in Boston, complete with a suit of armour that distorts Hester's letter into a monstrous size, and considers taking Pearl away from her mother for the child's spiritual good. He is the book's ordinary face of authority: not cruel, merely certain.
characters.clue: His polished breastplate makes the letter look enormous, and he has to be argued out of removing a child from her mother.

characters.name: Mistress Hibbins
characters.role: The Governor's sister, reputed a witch
characters.summary: She invites Hester to the forest to meet the Black Man, recognises Dimmesdale's condition on sight, and is later executed for witchcraft. Hawthorne uses her to leave one possibility open: the forest bargain the townspeople believe in is one the narrator will neither confirm nor rule out.
characters.clue: She keeps offering people a night ride to the forest, and is hanged for it in the end.

characters.name: The people of Boston
characters.summary: They open the book demanding a branding iron and close it deciding that the letter means Able and that the minister's confession was a parable. As a character they have one consistent trait: whatever they believe, they believe it unanimously and without memory of having believed anything else.
characters.clue: They gather at the same scaffold three times, and give three different verdicts without noticing that they have changed their minds.

themes.name: Public punishment
themes.summary: The sentence is not the prison term, which is already over when the book opens; it is being looked at for life. Hawthorne is precise about what that does: every errand Hester runs becomes a performance, strangers become an audience, and in the end the badge becomes a qualification, which is not the same as a pardon.
themes.development: From the scaffold hour in Chapter 2, through the years of errands in Chapter 13, to the voluntary resumption of the letter at the end, when there is no magistrate left to require it.

themes.name: Secrecy and the body
themes.summary: What is hidden in this book does not stay abstract: it gets into the chest, the complexion, the hand that keeps rising to the heart. Dimmesdale's concealment is treated as a medical condition with a physician in attendance, and the physician is the injured husband, which makes the diagnosis a form of torture.
themes.development: Announced in Chapter 11's account of a life so false it hollows out reality, staged at midnight in Chapter 12, and finally exhibited on the scaffold in Chapter 23 — where the witnesses cannot agree what they saw.

themes.name: The letter’s meaning
themes.summary: The magistrates intend the A as a fixed sentence; Hester's embroidery has already altered it before she leaves the prison. Over seven years the same three stitches are read as adultery, as ability, as an angel in the sky, and as a judgement on a minister's chest. Meaning is not infinite here — it is contested, and the contest has winners.
themes.development: Set up by the gold thread in Chapter 2, restated as a matter of town opinion in Chapter 13, and left unresolved in Chapter 24, which offers several accounts and does not choose between them.

themes.name: Revenge
themes.summary: Chillingworth does not strike; he settles in. The novel’s harshest judgement falls on a man who makes another person’s inner life his life’s work, far more than on the adultery, and it is put as a violation of the heart’s sanctuary, not as cruelty. When his subject dies he has nothing left and is gone within the year.
themes.development: Begins as a scholar's curiosity in Chapter 4, hardens into a profession by Chapter 10, and is named the blacker sin by Dimmesdale himself in Chapter 17.

themes.name: Town, forest and brook
themes.summary: The settlement is where the letter is enforced and the forest is where it can be taken off, but Hawthorne will not let the forest be simply free: it is also where Mistress Hibbins signs her book and where Hester admits her thinking has run wild. The brook between mother and child is the book's most exact piece of geography.
themes.development: The rosebush at the prison door in Chapter 1 sets the terms; Chapters 16 to 19 test them, and Pearl's refusal to cross the water withdraws the offer.

themes.name: Ancestors and offices
themes.summary: 'The Customhouse' puts two histories in front of the romance: a Salem judge in the family line, and the narrator's own appointment to a federal post. Both are ways of belonging to an institution that judges people, and the seventeenth-century story is written by a man uneasily aware that he has inherited the bench.
themes.development: Stated in the introductory sketch, carried into the fiction by magistrates who are never villains, and left with Pearl, who inherits a murderer's money and leaves the country.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: Presenting fiction as a document the narrator merely discovered and edited.
techniques.inThisBook: 'The Customhouse' produces a rag of cloth and Surveyor Pue's papers, gives the narrator a burn on the chest as authorisation, and never once pretends the reader should believe it.

techniques.name: Multiple explanations
techniques.definition: Offering natural and supernatural accounts of the same event without deciding between them.
techniques.inThisBook: The meteor in Chapter 12 is a sign, an optical effect, or a symptom of a diseased conscience; the mark on Dimmesdale's chest gets four separate explanations in Chapter 24, including the theory that there was nothing there.

techniques.name: The repeated tableau
techniques.definition: Staging the same arrangement of characters in the same place at intervals, so the changes register.
techniques.inThisBook: Three scaffold scenes — noon, midnight, noon — with the same three people and a different distribution of knowledge each time.

techniques.name: Emblem
techniques.definition: An object made to stand for an idea, in the tradition of the emblem book and the heraldic device.
techniques.inThisBook: The book ends on a coat of arms, ‘On a field, sable, the letter A, gules’: the punishment has become the formal blazon of a tombstone.

techniques.name: The intruding narrator
techniques.definition: A narrator who steps forward to generalise, moralise or admit uncertainty.
techniques.inThisBook: He tells us what Chillingworth's face is doing and then says he cannot be sure; he draws a moral in Chapter 24 and puts it in quotation marks, as if reporting somebody else's.

techniques.name: Symbolic names
techniques.definition: Giving characters names that carry a judgement or a quality.
techniques.inThisBook: A physician who chills, a minister whose name contains a dimming, and a child named for a thing of great price, bought by selling everything else.

quotations.text: which evidently found something congenial in the soil that had so early borne the black flower of civilized society, a prison
quotations.context: Describing the weeds on the grass-plot in front of the jail, in the book's opening paragraph.
quotations.analysis: The prison is called a flower, as though punishment grew out of settlement itself and was not a response to crime; the chapter has already noted that every new colony lays out a graveyard and a jail before anything else. The rosebush beside the door arrives one sentence later, so the book's first image is a pair of flowers, one of them a building.

quotations.text: On the breast of her gown, in fine red cloth, surrounded with an elaborate embroidery and fantastic flourishes of gold-thread, appeared the letter A.
quotations.context: Hester's first appearance, coming out of the prison door with Pearl in her arms.
quotations.analysis: The sentence puts four clauses of craftsmanship in front of the letter itself, so the reader meets the needlework before the charge. Hester has been given a sentence and has answered it with her trade: the gold thread exceeds what the magistrates ordered, which is why the goodwives in the crowd are so angry about it.

quotations.text: “I will not speak!” answered Hester, turning pale as death, but responding to this voice, which she too surely recognized. “And my child must seek a heavenly Father; she shall never know an earthly one!”
quotations.speaker: Hester Prynne
quotations.context: Refusing, from the scaffold, to name Pearl's father, after Dimmesdale has been ordered to exhort her.
quotations.analysis: The refusal is addressed to the man asking for it, and the narrator's aside — she recognised the voice — lets the reader in on the arrangement a hundred pages before the town gets there. Her second sentence is a legal fiction, more than defiance: a father invented to fill an empty space on a record, the same manoeuvre Dimmesdale will use for seven years.

quotations.text: It irks me, nevertheless, that the partner of her iniquity should not, at least, stand on the scaffold by her side. But he will be known!⁠—he will be known!⁠—he will be known!
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: Spoken by the stranger in the crowd, who has not yet given anyone his name.
quotations.analysis: Three identical clauses, and each one is a promise, not a prediction: he is describing work he intends to do. The irony is that he is standing in a crowd deciding not to be known himself, so the sentence that launches his revenge is also the moment he takes a false name.

quotations.text: she felt or fancied, then, that the scarlet letter had endowed her with a new sense
quotations.context: After Hester settles in a cottage on the edge of the settlement and begins to support herself by her needle.
quotations.analysis: ‘Felt or fancied’ is the book’s characteristic hedge, and it comes before the claim, not after it. The sense she acquires is a detector for concealed sin in respectable people, which is either a supernatural gift or the ordinary consequence of being the only person in town with nothing left to hide.

quotations.text: It was the scarlet letter in another form; the scarlet letter endowed with life!
quotations.context: Describing the crimson and gold tunic Hester has made for Pearl to wear to the Governor's hall.
quotations.analysis: Hester has dressed her daughter to match her own badge, which is either an act of defiance or a confession that she can no longer imagine the child apart from the crime. The exclamation mark belongs to the narrator, and it is worth noticing how often the adults in this book need Pearl to be a symbol, when she is a three-year-old with good clothes.

quotations.text: “God gave me the child!” cried she. “He gave her in requital of all things else, which ye had taken from me. She is my happiness!⁠—she is my torture, none the less! Pearl keeps me here in life! Pearl punishes me too!
quotations.speaker: Hester Prynne
quotations.context: Arguing against the magistrates' proposal to take Pearl away and have her brought up elsewhere.
quotations.analysis: She wins the argument by conceding the prosecution's case: yes, the child is a punishment, and that is the reason to leave her where she is. The two exclamations balance on the same verb, and the strategy is one Hester uses throughout — she never denies what the colony says about her, she simply refuses to draw its conclusions.

quotations.text: To the untrue man, the whole universe is false⁠—it is impalpable⁠—it shrinks to nothing within his grasp.
quotations.context: Explaining why Dimmesdale's visions of his dead parents and his congregation feel more solid to him than furniture.
quotations.analysis: The falsehood is described as spreading outward from the liar until it reaches the walls, which is a much stronger claim than that lying is wrong. It also explains the shape of Dimmesdale's sermons: the only thing he can still feel is the anguish, so the anguish is the only thing he can preach, and it is exactly what makes him beloved.

quotations.text: “Come up hither, Hester, thou and little Pearl,” said the Reverend Mr. Dimmesdale. “Ye have both been here before, but I was not with you. Come up hither once again, and we will stand all three together!”
quotations.speaker: Arthur Dimmesdale
quotations.context: On the scaffold at midnight, when no one in Boston is awake to see it.
quotations.analysis: Every word of this would be a confession at noon, and the sentence is grammatically identical to the one he will finally speak in Chapter 23. The only variable is the hour, which is the book's point about him: he has never lacked the words, only the daylight.

quotations.text: many people refused to interpret the scarlet A by its original signification. They said that it meant Able; so strong was Hester Prynne, with a woman’s strength.
quotations.context: After seven years of nursing the sick and clothing the poor.
quotations.analysis: The town has not forgiven her; it has relabelled her, which is cheaper. Note the passive shape of the reading — 'they said that it meant' — and note that the letter itself has not moved an inch: the same three stitches now certify a virtue, so the badge has proved capable of holding whatever the community needs it to hold.

quotations.text: Thou hadst great elements. Peradventure, hadst thou met earlier with a better love than mine, this evil had not been. I pity thee, for the good that has been wasted in thy nature!
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: By the shore, when Hester tells him she means to break her promise of secrecy.
quotations.analysis: It is the fairest judgement anyone passes on Hester and it comes from the man ruining her lover, which is the novel's way of showing that accuracy is not the same as goodness. The conditional in the middle sentence also admits what the whole plot depends on: a marriage arranged between an old scholar and a young woman is where the evil actually started.

quotations.text: Ye that have wronged me are not sinful, save in a kind of typical illusion; neither am I fiend-like, who have snatched a fiend’s office from his hands. It is our fate. Let the black flower blossom as it may!
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: Refusing Hester's suggestion that he forgive, in the same conversation.
quotations.analysis: He describes his own vocation in the language of employment — he has taken over a post that belonged to a fiend — and then abolishes all responsibility by calling it fate. The image returns from the first page, where the prison was a black flower growing out of the soil of settlement; here revenge is a plant too, and the gardener denies having planted it.

quotations.text: Let men tremble to win the hand of woman, unless they win along with it the utmost passion of her heart!
quotations.context: The narrator, after Hester admits to herself that she hates her husband.
quotations.analysis: The warning is addressed to men in general and delivered in the imperative, which is as close as this narrator comes to taking a side. It also moves the novel’s original sin from the forest to the wedding: the marriage was contracted without the wife’s heart, and everything after it follows.

quotations.text: “Mother,” said little Pearl, “the sunshine does not love you. It runs away and hides itself, because it is afraid of something on your bosom. Now, see! There it is, playing, a good way off. Stand you here, and let me run and catch it. I am but a child. It will not flee from me; for I wear nothing on my bosom yet!”
quotations.speaker: Pearl
quotations.context: On the forest path, walking to the meeting with Dimmesdale.
quotations.analysis: A child's observation about where the light happens to fall becomes the most efficient statement of the book's premise, and the last word does the damage: 'yet' assumes she will wear one in time. Pearl has worked out the rule of her mother's world without being told it, and she expects to inherit it.

quotations.text: “Never, never!” whispered she. “What we did had a consecration of its own. We felt it so! We said so to each other! Hast thou forgotten it?”
quotations.speaker: Hester Prynne
quotations.context: Answering Dimmesdale's question whether they are past hope.
quotations.analysis: She uses the vocabulary of the church to describe the act the church punished, and the tense is the point, ‘had’ where it might have been ‘has’: she is defending the past, not proposing a future. In 1850 this was the sentence reviewers objected to, and the novel neither retracts it nor lets her act on it.

quotations.text: There is one worse than even the polluted priest! That old man’s revenge has been blacker than my sin. He has violated, in cold blood, the sanctity of a human heart. Thou and I, Hester, never did so!
quotations.speaker: Arthur Dimmesdale
quotations.context: On learning that his physician and lodger is Hester's husband.
quotations.analysis: This is the moral scale the novel actually uses, and it is delivered by the man with the most to gain from it. 'In cold blood' is the operative phrase: the adultery is not excused, it is reclassified as a warm-blooded fault, while the sin the book cannot forgive is the deliberate, patient occupation of somebody else's inner life.

quotations.text: The scarlet letter was her passport into regions where other women dared not tread. Shame, Despair, Solitude! These had been her teachers⁠—stern and wild ones⁠—and they had made her strong, but taught her much amiss.
quotations.context: Explaining why Hester can contemplate flight and Dimmesdale cannot.
quotations.analysis: A punishment is redescribed as a travel document, which is the boldest reversal in the book — and then the final clause takes most of it back. 'Taught her much amiss' is the narrator declining to endorse his own heroine, and readers have been arguing ever since about whether that is Hawthorne's caution or Hawthorne's honesty.

quotations.text: The mystic token alighted on the hither verge of the stream. With a hand’s breadth farther flight it would have fallen into the water
quotations.context: Immediately after Hester unfastens the letter and throws it away among the leaves.
quotations.analysis: The narrator measures the miss in inches, which is the cruellest sentence in the chapter: the letter lands on this side of the brook, still retrievable, and so the whole flood of sunshine that follows is provisional. Pearl will make her pick it up within the hour, and the geography has already said she will have to.

quotations.text: “Is not this better,” murmured he, “than what we dreamed of in the forest?”
quotations.speaker: Arthur Dimmesdale
quotations.context: To Hester, as she supports him up the scaffold steps in front of the whole colony.
quotations.analysis: He is asking her to agree that public death is preferable to private escape, and she does not answer. The question is the last of his half-confessions: even at the end he needs the other person to pronounce the verdict, and Hawthorne withholds her reply so that the reader has to make it instead.

quotations.text: “Thou hast escaped me!” he repeated more than once. “Thou hast escaped me!”
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: Kneeling beside the scaffold as Dimmesdale confesses.
quotations.analysis: The verb makes the physician a gaoler, not an avenger, which is what he has been for seven years: his aim was always to keep the man, more than to punish him. Within a year Chillingworth is dead, and the book says plainly that he had nothing else left to do, which is as close as it comes to defining what revenge costs the avenger.

quotations.text: Be true! Be true! Be true! Show freely to the world, if not your worst, yet some trait whereby the worst may be inferred!
quotations.context: The moral the narrator draws from Dimmesdale's case, and puts in quotation marks.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives and then an immediate discount: not the worst, only enough of a hint that the worst could be worked out. It is a morality of adequate disclosure, which is less than honesty, and the narrator has just spent a chapter reporting four incompatible accounts of the minister’s chest, which suggests he knows how little inference can be trusted.

quotations.text: Here had been her sin; here, her sorrow; and here was yet to be her penitence.
quotations.context: Explaining why Hester comes back to the cottage on the edge of Boston years after she was free to leave.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses on the same adverb, and the tenses walk forward through them — had been, was, was yet to be — and a place becomes a chronology. The return is voluntary: the narrator notes that not the sternest magistrate would have required it, which makes the letter, at the very end, the only thing she has ever chosen to wear.

quotations.text: “On a field, sable, the letter A, gules.”
quotations.context: The last line of the book: the device carved on the slab that covers Hester and Dimmesdale.
quotations.analysis: The novel ends in heraldic French, a language of inherited honour, applied to a mark of shame — and the two words for the colours, black and red, are the only description of the grave we get. A punishment has become a coat of arms, which is either the final rehabilitation of the letter or proof that it will outlast everyone who tried to fix its meaning.

quotations.text: it seemed to me, then, that I experienced a sensation not altogether physical, yet almost so, of burning heat; and as if the letter were not of red cloth, but red-hot iron. I shuddered, and involuntarily let it fall upon the floor.
quotations.context: The narrator places the found scrap of embroidery on his own chest in the disused upper room of the Salem custom house.
quotations.analysis: The hedging is doing serious work — not altogether physical, yet almost so — and it establishes the rule for every marvel in the romance that follows. A man who will not commit himself to a sensation he has just had is the right narrator for a book whose final chapter cannot decide whether there was anything on Dimmesdale's chest at all.

quotations.text: the floor of our familiar room has become a neutral territory, somewhere between the real world and fairyland, where the Actual and the Imaginary may meet, and each imbue itself with the nature of the other
quotations.context: Describing moonlight in a room he cannot write in, near the end of the introductory sketch.
quotations.analysis: This is Hawthorne defining the romance as a form before he writes one, and the capital letters on Actual and Imaginary make it a diagram, not a mood. It also explains why the novel offers two explanations for almost everything: a neutral territory has to remain neutral, and a narrator who settled the meteor would have surrendered the ground.

timeline.label: The novel's opening scene, set about 1642
timeline.detail: The novel places Pearl's birth in the early 1640s, some fifteen or twenty years after the settlement of Boston.

timeline.label: Governor John Winthrop dies
timeline.detail: The historical death the novel puts on the night of Dimmesdale's midnight vigil, with a meteor over the town.

timeline.label: The Salem witch trials
timeline.detail: John Hathorne sat as one of the examining magistrates; the novelist added a w to the family name.

timeline.label: Nathaniel Hawthorne born in Salem
timeline.detail: His father, a ship's captain, died in Surinam four years later.

timeline.label: Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales published
timeline.detail: The collection that made his name among writers, if not yet among book-buyers.

timeline.label: Hawthorne is appointed Surveyor of the Port of Salem
timeline.detail: Three years in the custom house gave him the material for the book's introductory sketch.

timeline.label: Hawthorne loses his custom-house post, and his mother dies
timeline.detail: The dismissal followed a change of administration; the romance was written in the months after both events.

timeline.label: The Scarlet Letter is published in Boston
timeline.detail: Ticknor, Reed and Fields issued it in March; it sold out quickly enough to need a second printing straight away.

timeline.label: Second edition, with Hawthorne's new preface
timeline.detail: Salem had taken 'The Customhouse' personally, and Hawthorne declined to withdraw a word of it.

timeline.label: Hawthorne's The House of the Seven Gables published
timeline.detail: Written in the Berkshires, where Melville was his neighbour and about to dedicate Moby-Dick to him.

timeline.label: Hawthorne dies at Plymouth, New Hampshire
timeline.detail: He was buried at Sleepy Hollow Cemetery in Concord, Massachusetts.

timeline.label: Victor Sjöström films the novel with Lillian Gish as Hester
timeline.detail: The silent version fixed a popular image of the story that stayed in circulation for decades.

places.name: Salem, Massachusetts
places.note: Hawthorne's birthplace, the custom house of the frame, and the town his ancestor judged witches in.

places.name: Boston, Massachusetts
places.note: The colonial settlement of the romance: prison, marketplace, scaffold, Governor's hall and meeting-house.

places.name: King's Chapel Burying Ground
places.note: The old churchyard named in the first chapter, and the kind of ground the final slab belongs to.

places.name: Amsterdam
places.note: Where Hester and her husband lived before she sailed ahead of him to Massachusetts.

places.name: Concord, Massachusetts
places.note: The Old Manse, where Hawthorne wrote before Salem, and the cemetery where he was buried.

places.name: Lenox, Massachusetts
places.note: The Berkshire cottage he moved to months after publication, and where Melville rode over to see him.

criticalViews.summary: The longest-standing reading takes the book's subject to be what secrecy does to a mind and a body, with Dimmesdale as the case and Chillingworth as the pathology of the observer.
criticalViews.counter: It tends to make Hester the occasion for two men's inner lives, when she is the only character in the book who acts.

criticalViews.summary: Read with ‘The Customhouse’ attached, the novel is a nineteenth-century writer negotiating with a Puritan ancestry — a judge in the family, a federal post of his own — more than a reconstruction of the 1640s.
criticalViews.counter: The frame can be treated as so decisive that the seventeenth-century story becomes merely illustrative, which is not how it reads.

criticalViews.position: A book about the government of women
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the 1970s has concentrated on Hester's needle as the only economic independence available to her, on the magistrates' proposal to remove her child, and on the closing prophecy of a truth that could not be entrusted to a woman stained with sin.
criticalViews.counter: The final chapter's retreat — Hester returns, resumes the badge, and defers the revelation to someone purer — is hard to read as either endorsement or critique, and both sides claim it.

criticalViews.summary: The A is read half a dozen ways by half a dozen parties, the meteor gets three explanations, and the minister's chest gets four. On this account the romance is about communities deciding what marks mean, and the power that decision carries.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed far enough, it leaves a novel with real suffering in it looking like an essay on signs.

essayQuestions.question: How does Hawthorne use the three scaffold scenes to structure the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Repetition, staging and the distribution of knowledge
plan: Set the three scenes side by side: Chapter 2 at noon, Chapter 12 at midnight, Chapter 23 at noon again.
Track who is present, who is watching, and who knows what at each of the three points.
Show that Dimmesdale's midnight words are nearly identical to his final ones, so the variable is the audience.
Use Chillingworth's position in each scene — in the crowd, at the foot, kneeling — to measure his progress.
Close on what the third scene fails to settle: the witnesses in Chapter 24 cannot agree what they saw.

essayQuestions.question: 'The letter changes meaning, but never stops working.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: The unstable sign and the power behind it
plan: Begin with the gold thread in Chapter 2: Hester alters the sentence before she has served an hour of it.
Trace the readings — adultery, Able, an angel in the sky, a mark on a minister's chest.
Note who does the reading each time, and that the object itself never changes.
Test the case with Chapter 18, where the letter comes off and the forest brightens, and Chapter 19, where it goes back on.
Decide what it means that Hester resumes the badge when nobody is enforcing it.

essayQuestions.question: Is Chillingworth the villain of The Scarlet Letter?
essayQuestions.focus: Revenge, marriage and the ethics of observation
plan: Establish the facts he is right about, and the accuracy of his diagnosis in Chapter 10.
Use Chapter 14 to show him passing the fairest judgement anyone passes on Hester.
Set against that Dimmesdale's verdict in Chapter 17 — the violation of a human heart in cold blood.
Consider the marriage itself, and Chapter 15's warning to men who win a hand without a heart.
Weigh the conclusion: he dies within the year and leaves his property to the child of the man he destroyed.

essayQuestions.question: What does 'The Customhouse' do for the romance that follows?
essayQuestions.focus: Frame, provenance and the claims a romance makes
plan: Describe what the sketch claims: a scrap of cloth, Surveyor Pue's papers, a burn on the chest.
Note that all of it is invented, and that the sketch tells us so by its tone.
Use the moonlit room and the neutral territory as Hawthorne's own definition of the form.
Connect the narrator's ancestry and his federal office to the magistrates in the story.
Ask what would be lost if a modern edition printed the twenty-four chapters alone.

discussionQuestions: Hester is punished, Dimmesdale is revered, and Chillingworth is free. Does the ending correct any of that, or only end it?
Pearl is called a demon, an elf and the scarlet letter given life. What happens if you read her simply as a child?
The novel never dramatises the adultery. Why does Hawthorne begin after it, and what would change if he had not?
Chapter 24 gives four accounts of what was on Dimmesdale's chest, including the claim that there was nothing. Which one does the book prefer?
The forest lets the letter come off and the brook puts it back. Is nature on Hester's side in this book?
Hester says what they did had a consecration of its own. Does the novel ever answer her?

related.why: Dedicated to Hawthorne a year later by a neighbour who had just read this book, and the other great American argument with a symbol.
The same case tried in England fifty years on: a woman marked by an event and judged for the rest of her life.
A later American novel about a woman whose independence is available only outside the settled community.
Another study of a first-person conscience formed against an institution, and of a secret kept inside a respectable house.
The other American book about a conscience that has been trained wrong by the community it belongs to.
